body.heading: Happy and sad are just the beginning
paragraphs: Ask most people how they feel and you will hear 'fine', 'good', 'happy' or 'sad'. But real feelings are much more specific — and specific words are powerful. 'I feel frustrated' tells people exactly what is wrong. 'I feel bad' does not.
Here is a bigger toolkit. Every word below is a feeling you have probably already had.

body.heading: Proud, grateful, excited, calm
paragraphs: Proud — I practiced for weeks and it worked. My chest feels full.
Grateful — Someone did something kind for me, and I notice it and appreciate it.
Excited — Something good is coming and my body feels buzzy and awake.
Calm — My breathing is slow, my shoulders are down, nothing needs fixing right now.

body.heading: Frustrated, nervous, disappointed, left out
paragraphs: Frustrated — I keep trying and it keeps not working. (Frustration often means you need a break or a new strategy — not that you are bad at it.)
Nervous — Something important is coming and my stomach feels fluttery. Almost everyone feels this before performances and first days.
Disappointed — I hoped for one thing and got another. The hope was real, so the let-down is real too.
Left out — Others are together and I am not included. Naming it honestly is the first step to changing it.

body.heading: Brave and embarrassed
paragraphs: Brave — I am scared AND I am doing it anyway. Brave is not the absence of fear; it is fear with its boots on.
Embarrassed — Everyone saw my mistake and my face feels hot. It fades faster than it feels like it will — and everyone has been there.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Which word from this chart fits your day best right now? Say it in a full sentence: 'I feel ___ because…'.
2. Which feeling word do you think adults need to hear more often — and why?

takeaway: Precise feelings words — proud, frustrated, nervous, grateful, left out, brave — turn 'I feel bad' into information other people can actually help with.
materials: Just you and this page — no materials needed
supervision: A grown-up nearby is recommended for younger readers; the think-and-talk questions work well read aloud together.
